21.0.0.en: Jezreel: a city lying in the plain of Jezreel, which extends from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the Jordan River in the east. Its climate is pleasant and suited to the winter season, and it is 32 km from Samaria.

21.0.1.en: After Israel's victory over Aram, Ahab's release of Ben-hadad and God's rebuke of him, he became depressed and went to his palace in Jezreel to rest, and tried to cheer himself up. He looked beside his palace and found a field owned by Naboth the Jezreelite, a man who believed in God and held fast to the Law, as will appear from (v. 4), and who was one of the seven thousand knees that had not bowed to Baal (19:18). Ahab wished to take this field and make it a garden belonging to his palace.

21.1.0.en: Ahab called Naboth and asked him to give up his field to him, because he wanted to make it a private garden for himself and plant some vegetables in it. Perhaps Ahab wanted to cheer himself with this garden so as to get out of his depression. He offered Naboth two proposals:

21.1.2.en: 1- To give him another vineyard from the king's possessions in place of this vineyard, and he was even ready to give him a better vineyard than this one.

21.1.3.en: 2- To give him the price of this vineyard in an amount of silver.

21.1.4.en: In all this Ahab forgot that the Law ordains that no one should give up his field, the inheritance of his fathers, and if he is forced to mortgage it because he needs money, it returns to him in the year of Jubilee (Lev 25:23-24). This offer seems fair, but it does not agree with God's Law, because Ahab did not care about God or His Law. By this request he broke the tenth commandment, which says, "Thou shalt not covet ... any thing that is thy neighbour's" (Ex 20:17).

21.2.0.en: Naboth was very distressed when he heard King Ahab's request and refused to give him his vineyard, for the following reasons:

21.2.1.en: 1- Because Naboth was a godly man who held fast to God's Law, which stipulates that a person must hold fast to the inheritance of his fathers in the land, because it is a gift from God that cannot be squandered, and it is a type of the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

21.2.2.en: 2- The land bears the memories of the fathers and forefathers who toiled in it and took care of it.

21.2.3.en: 3- Naboth refused Ahab's words because he understood that the king would take the land and would not return it to him again, for it was not like other lands that can be mortgaged and then recovered after a while. Therefore Naboth's refusal was decisive, and this shows not only Naboth's faith but also his courage.

21.2.4.en: Be strong in holding fast to your spiritual practices and your relationship with the Church, however much circumstances press upon you or others try to distract you from them, however logical your justifications. Your relationship with God and the salvation of your soul are more important than anything. Be courageous in holding fast to your right to life with God.

21.3.0.en: If Ahab had been depressed by the words of the prophet, who told him that he would die because he released Ben-hadad, and had tried to cheer himself and rejoice in the desire to own Naboth's vineyard, now he returns to his depression a second time because Naboth refused his request. So Ahab went into his chamber and lay down on his bed in sorrow with his face to the wall, and refused to eat. This shows the following:

21.3.1.en: 1- The weakness of Ahab's character and his agitation over any small matter, which is not fitting for a king.

21.3.2.en: 2- The mastermind of the kingdom was his wife Jezebel, as will appear from the following verses, and this shows that the cause of the spread of idol worship in the kingdom was Jezebel, using Ahab's weakness and indifference.

21.3.3.en: 3- Material desires give only a temporary pleasure, then they pass away, and losing them brings sorrow upon a person. They are not the means that give joy and peace, but a temporary deception by which a person thinks he can make himself rejoice. Ahab was a man of pleasure who tried to delight himself with possessions and buildings, as he built a house of ivory (ch. 22:39), and at the same time he quickly became depressed, but did no useful work and did not return to God.

21.4.0.en: Jezebel learned from the king's servants that he had refused to eat and had gone into his bedchamber sad, and perhaps some of them told her what they had heard of his conversation with Naboth. So she hurried to his chamber and found him sunk in his sorrow, and she asked him in astonishment why he was sad, because with her strong personality these small matters did not affect her, in addition to the fact that she used her wicked means to reach her ends, so these small problems did not stand in her way. This shows the strength of her personality and that she in truth was the one running this kingdom and not Ahab.

21.5.0.en: Ahab expressed the depression that he had stored up in his heart and told his wife the reason for his sorrow, which was Naboth's refusal to give him his vineyard. Of course he did not mention that this was contrary to the Law, because Naboth had said, "The LORD forbid it me ...", and this is because Ahab did not care about God's commandments or His Law.

21.6.0.en: Jezebel rebuked her husband for his weakness and slackness in using his authority as king to get what he wanted, since she believed that the king's authority is absolute and is not subject to any god or law. By this she stirred up Ahab's pride, then reassured him that she would give him Naboth's vineyard, so let him arise, eat and rejoice, for what he desired was sure to be obtained. This shows:

21.6.1.en: 1- How strong Jezebel's personality was, for she carried out what she wanted in the whole kingdom.

21.6.2.en: 2- How great Jezebel's wickedness was, for she used any means, however wicked, to achieve her ends, as will appear in the following verses, since she respected no law; what she wanted had to be done.

21.6.3.en: 3- How weak Ahab was, since he could not argue with her and accepted her rebuke cowardly, and did not even ask her how she would give him the vineyard, for he was completely subject to her and left to her the management of the kingdom as she wished.

21.7.0.en: Belial: a Hebrew word meaning without profit, or worthless, and it is also used to express Satan, so the sons of Belial are the sons of evil and of worthlessness and of Satan.

21.7.1.en: Jezebel used the king's seal, which was in her hand because the king was subject to her. She sent letters to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city and sealed them with the king's seal, that is, they were royal orders, in which she asked them to proclaim a fast in the city, meaning that a great problem had befallen the city and its solution was to take refuge in God by fasting, that He might lift from the city what had befallen it. So she deceives and plays the hypocrite and appears as if she were religious, calling for a fast, and as if she also cared for the cities of the kingdom and solved their problems. Then she demanded with all impudence that they bring two wicked men to bear false witness against Naboth that he had blasphemed God and the king, who is God's deputy and the executor of His commands (Ex 22:28). Blasphemy means that he spoke wicked words against God and the king. This was to be in a public council gathering the elders and great men of the city, and they were to seat Naboth in a prominent place, visible, to be tried, that is, it would be a lawful court, and they would accuse Naboth in it of blasphemy and sentence him to death by stoning (Lev 24:16, Jn 10:33). Jezebel's cruelty appears in that she also commanded the killing of Naboth's sons (2 Kgs 9:26), so that he would have no heir, and his property would pass to the state, that is, the king, in addition to the fact that he was considered a servant of the king, so his property would be given to the king (2 Sam 16:4). And of course she arranged an accusation against them, that they shared with him in the blasphemy, so they also deserved death.

21.7.3.en: 1- That she had studied the Law, so she was careful to bring two witnesses, for one witness is not sufficient (Deut 17:6).

21.7.4.en: 2- That she was wicked and very cruel, regarding the killing of people as permissible.

21.7.5.en: 3- That she was deceitful, adorning herself in the garb of spirituality and of holding fast to the worship of God and caring for her people, while she was as far from this as could be.

21.8.0.en: The elders and nobles of the city of Jezreel, that is, the leaders of the city, carried out Jezebel's words exactly and stoned Naboth, and this shows the following:

21.8.1.en: 1- Their great fear of the cruel, violent Jezebel.

21.8.2.en: 2- Perhaps they were hoping for her favor or for some gains from her.

21.8.3.en: And Naboth here is a type of Christ, who was wronged, and they bore false witness against Him and killed Him, although He was completely innocent. The Second Book of Kings

21.9.0.en: The elders of the city informed Jezebel that they had carried out her words and killed Naboth, and she rejoiced because she had completed her plan, and went to Ahab to tell him of Naboth's death and to give him the good news that he had become the owner of the vineyard without paying anything; that is, she had easily achieved his desire for him. This shows how little she regarded people's lives, and her violent wickedness and selfishness.

21.10.0.en: Ahab rejoiced that Naboth's vineyard had become his, and in his joy he went down himself to inspect this vineyard and see what he wanted to make of it, to enjoy himself with the pleasures of life. This shows his immersion in his pleasures and his joy and submission to his wife, that is, his conviction that she was running the kingdom well, because she had fulfilled his desire. It also shows that he was selfish, not caring about what had happened to Naboth, but the important thing was that he had come to own the vineyard.

21.10.1.en: Do not rejoice in obtaining your desires unless it is in a sound way that does not violate God's commandments, because every pleasure is temporary and passing, and you cannot gain happiness on earth except by following God's commandments, and afterward you gain the joys of the Kingdom.

21.11.s.en: (3) The punishment of Ahab and Jezebel

21.11.0.en: God was greatly angered by the injustice of Jezebel and Ahab and their killing of Naboth and his family, so He spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, to leave the wilderness and go down to Jezreel, to Naboth's vineyard, to meet Ahab, who reigns in his capital Samaria.

21.11.1.en: And we notice two things in this:

21.11.2.en: 1- That God summons Elijah to service more than five years after his weakness and his flight from the face of Jezebel, after he killed the prophets of Baal. After he spent a period of seclusion in the wilderness and regained his spiritual and psychological strength, God renews his vigor and calls him to service, and this shows God's pleasure with him. Therefore He calls him as He called him at the beginning of his ministry (1 Kgs 17:1), as Elijah the Tishbite, that is, he starts anew, for God had forgiven him his weakness and called him to a new service. Elijah's virtues appear in that he obeyed at once and did not fear Ahab or Jezebel and did not flee from Jezebel as the first time, although the message was very difficult, for he informs the king that he, his wife and all his descendants will die.

21.11.3.en: 2- That God is jealous for His believing children, that is, Naboth, and sends the greatest of the prophets at that time, Elijah, and not an ordinary prophet as He sent to Ahab during his war with Ben-hadad.

21.12.0.en: When Elijah met Ahab, fear covered Ahab's face, because he had not seen Elijah for more than five years, since the time he killed the prophets of Baal who followed him, and because Ahab felt that he had erred in taking possession of Naboth's vineyard, even if he and Jezebel tried to forget their fault. In front of Elijah, who of course represented God, Ahab was afraid.

21.12.1.en: Elijah declared to Ahab the grounds of the sentence against him, that is, the reasons for the divine punishment of him. These reasons are his killing of Naboth, then his seizing his vineyard, that is, his inheriting his vineyard without right. Although Ahab did not himself order Naboth to be killed, he is responsible for his killing, because he left authority to his wicked wife to do what she wanted. The divine punishment included two things:

21.12.3.en: 1- That as Ahab killed, Ahab too will be killed.

21.12.4.en: 2- As the dogs licked the blood of Naboth in Jezreel, the dogs will lick the blood of Ahab. And this is what actually happened, for Ahab was killed in his war with Aram and the dogs licked his blood in the same place where Naboth died, that is, in Jezreel (ch. 22:38). Licking the blood is a kind of contempt, and this signifies what will happen in the eternal torment of the wicked, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

21.12.5.en: And we see how Elijah regained his strength to deliver to Ahab a severe message of rebuke, than which there is none harder, for with courage he told him that he would die a shameful death.

21.13.0.en: After Ahab heard God's judgment upon him, his fear and agitation increased, and in weakness he said to Elijah:

21.13.1.en: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" For he feels that he is walking in evil and rejecting God by his worship of idols, so God is against him and his enemy, and God's representative is Elijah; and whoever befriends Satan of course has God as his enemy, because the worship of idols is the worship of demons, just as the thief says to the police officer, "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?", since he knows that he is a criminal who deserves punishment.

21.13.2.en: But Elijah made clear to him that the problem was within him, for he had sold himself to evil, that is, he had made sin permissible and his heart was no longer moved to repent, so he became sold, that is, enslaved to evil. Ahab sold himself by himself, for he chose evil and rejected God. And Elijah represents the conscience, that is, the voice of God that alerted Ahab to his sin, for as soon as Ahab saw Elijah he was alarmed and remembered his sin. On the other hand, whoever declares the truth to those who err is hated by them, but he declares it for God's sake and in obedience to Him.

21.14.0.en: Him that pisseth against the wall: a male, whether a child or an adult.

21.14.1.en: Shut up: an old man unable to go out or bound in one of the prisons.

21.14.2.en: Left: a young man who goes out and moves about much, or a free person who is not bound.

21.14.3.en: Elijah paid no attention to Ahab's objection but continued God's punishment of him, that perhaps he would take notice and repent. He said to him that God would bring evil upon you and all your descendants would be destroyed, especially the males, whether adults or children, who could succeed you in the kingship, that is, He would cut the kingship off from your house.

21.14.4.en: This total destruction proclaims God's great anger at Ahab's persistence in evil. And strangely, this destruction was carried out by King Jehu, who was one of Ahab's military commanders and was present when Ahab took possession of Naboth's field (2 Kgs 9:25), and when he became king he was extremely violent in destroying Ahab's descendants. Perhaps Jehu heard God's sentence on Ahab from the mouth of Elijah, because he was one of those close to King Ahab.

21.15.0.en: God confirms through Elijah's mouth that the total destruction of all Ahab's descendants will be like the destruction of the descendants of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the first king of Israel, who introduced idol worship into the kingdom by making the two golden calves. Then Baasha reigned after that, who destroyed the descendants of Jeroboam, not out of love for God or to stop idol worship, but so that he would have no rival, and he left idol worship as it was; therefore God destroyed his descendants by the hand of King Zimri (ch. 14:10, 11, 16:3-4). These are historical events that Ahab knew well, and Elijah declared them to him, that perhaps he would repent and leave idol worship and remove it from the kingdom, otherwise God would not go back on His word and would destroy his descendants, because he encouraged the worship of Baal and Ashtaroth, and in addition to that he killed God's prophets.

21.16.0.en: Rampart (wall): a wall built outside the city for fortification, that is, set at the border of the city. God's punishment also included the source of corruption in the kingdom, the pagan Jezebel, who encouraged idol worship and killed God's prophets, using the name of her husband Ahab to do every evil. God said that she would die at the border of Jezreel and the dogs would eat her corpse in the same region in which Naboth was killed. This actually happened by the hand of King Jehu, and the dogs left of her nothing but the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands (2 Kgs 9:35).

21.16.1.en: Whoever seizes another's right, or covets what is not his, will have a terrible result like Ahab and Jezebel. So set limits to your looks, your thoughts and your words, and do not covet what belongs to another, because God's punishment is stern, and it is eternal torment. And if you have fallen into these desires, set your affairs right by repentance, and if you have taken anything from anyone, you must return it to him.

21.17.0.en: God makes clear that Ahab's descendants will die without honor, although they are of royal seed. No funerals or lamentations will be made for them, but they will be thrown on the ground, and the wild dogs in the city will eat them, and whoever is killed in the field will be eaten by the birds of prey.

21.18.0.en: Ahab was the most wicked of the kings of Israel, for the following reasons:

21.18.1.en: 1- He encouraged idol worship and injustice, knowing that this was wrong.

21.18.2.en: 2- He regarded this evil as permissible, defying God, and did it before the eyes of the LORD.

21.18.3.en: 3- He was not excusable, but sold himself of his own will and enslaved himself to this evil, that Satan might do with him what he wished.

21.18.4.en: 4- He was led along and convinced to submit to his wicked wife Jezebel, who seduced him to do all evils; he was weak in character yet at the same time completely given over to her, so his evil increased.

21.19.0.en: Did abominably: that is, became filthy; this is the linguistic origin of the word, but with time what was meant by it was that he was immersed in uncleanness and evil.

21.19.1.en: Ahab imitated the Amorites, the original inhabitants of the Promised Land, who were the strongest of the Canaanite tribes and lived in the mountains, as the inhabitants of Samaria and what belonged to it lived in the mountains. So Ahab worshiped idols and spread this worship in his kingdom, with all the debauchery and unclean desires connected with it, imitating the Amorites, and so he became very unclean. And as God destroyed the Amorites from the land of Canaan because of their abomination, God destroys Ahab's descendants because he imitated them.

21.20.0.en: When Ahab heard from Elijah God's punishment of him, he was deeply moved, and this appeared in a number of things:

21.20.1.en: 1- He rent his clothes, as a sign of the dreadfulness of the news he had heard and of his great sorrow and remorse.

21.20.2.en: 2- He changed his splendid royal garments and put on sackcloth, that is, coarse clothing, which suits austerity and humbling oneself before God.

21.20.3.en: 3- He fasted, as a declaration of his rejection of the pleasures of the world and evil desires and of his drawing near to God.

21.20.4.en: 4- He lay in sackcloth, that is, he continued wearing sackcloth even while sleeping, as a sign of his continuing to humble himself before God. Perhaps the sackcloth prevented him from sleeping, so he prayed, asking God's forgiveness.

21.20.5.en: 5- He went softly, from his fear of God and his remorse and his deep sorrow over his sins that had caused him all this punishment. Perhaps he was reviewing himself about all that he had done. This great emotion is a sign of clear repentance.

21.20.6.en: But sadly it was a temporary repentance and a passing emotion, as is proved by:

21.20.7.en: 1- That he did not return Naboth's vineyard to one of his relatives, or give it to God, because it was seized and stolen, and it was not his right to keep it.

21.20.8.en: 2- His greed to own cities of the Arameans, for he stirred up war against them without reason (ch. 22:3).

21.20.9.en: 3- He consulted the false prophets, the prophets of Baal, to enter the war with Aram (ch. 22:6).

21.20.10.en: 4- He rejected God's word by the mouth of the prophet Micaiah, not to enter the war with Aram, but was angry with Micaiah and put him in prison (ch. 22:27). This confirms that sin was rooted in his life and that his remorse was temporary.

21.20.11.en: Do not let your repentance be a mere emotion, but make resolutions for repentance and try to carry them out carefully, so that the fruits of repentance appear in your life as a sign of God's acceptance of your repentance.

21.21.0.en: When Ahab did all these signs of repentance, God said to Elijah: since Ahab has shown his repentance, even though it is a temporary emotion, I will reward him by postponing the punishment to the days of his son. So Ahab died a shameful death in his war with the Arameans after three years (ch. 22), then all of Ahab's descendants were destroyed in the days of his son Jehoram by Jehu (2 Kgs 9, 10). And so we see God's mercies, which take into account even any signs of repentance, however temporary, to give Ahab an opportunity to complete his repentance. But sadly he learned nothing.

21.21.1.en: And by God's foreknowledge that Jehoram, Ahab's son, would be wicked, He allowed the destruction of all Ahab's descendants in his days. The death of Ahab
